auroc: Glucose below 70 mg/dL within 60 min: 0.88 [0.75, 0.96] (only 8 patients had events: limited evidence)
coverage: 80% intervals contained the true glucose 81 % of the time at +60 min (95% interval 78 to 84 %), median width 48 mg/dL. In the worst-covered patient the share was 58 %.
limitations: Coverage is not equal across groups: on CGMacros the intervals covered 87 % of healthy rows but 73 % of type 2 diabetes rows (Part 6).
A sensor that reads too high or drifts is not detected by the data-quality score, and coverage falls sharply under such faults.

The learned models understate the effect of carbohydrate: in matched real breakfasts they predicted about half of the observed rise, and the pre-registered dose-response test failed for both machine-learning models.
The twin adds little on top of the machine-learning model, and only the basal glucose Gb of the twin is identifiable from the data.
The static clinical profile did not improve the machine-learning forecasts; heart rate and activity add nothing measurable.
Low-glucose results rest on few events (8 patients in CGMacros) and are limited evidence.
All demonstration patients come from one open dataset of 45 people; no prospective or clinical validation was done. This is a research prototype, not a medical device.
limits_whatif: It cannot tell you what the patient will actually do or eat, only what the models predict for the change you enter.
It does not know about insulin or other medication doses, illness, stress or sleep.
Carbohydrate effects are understated by the learned models (about half of the observed rise in matched real breakfasts); treat the size of any change as a lower bound.
A walk can only be added 15 min after a meal for 30 min, the one setting that was tested.

figures.title: Which inputs help
figures.caption: Removing the CGM history hurts most. Adding wearable data or the clinical profile did not improve the forecasts.

figures.title: Do 80% intervals contain the truth?
figures.caption: Pooled coverage is close to 80 %, but it is not equal for all groups, and one method undercovered on the second cohort.

figures.title: Alert burden
figures.caption: How many episodes each alert catches for a given number of false alarms a day.

figures.title: What-if plausibility checks
figures.caption: Pass rates of physiological checks. The monotone model passes the carbohydrate and walk checks by construction.

figures.title: Matched real breakfasts
figures.caption: Predicted against observed peak difference in 87 matched pairs. The models understate the rise.

figures.title: Learning from a patient's first days
figures.caption: Fine-tuning on the patient's own data lowers the error by about 1 mg/dL after 3 to 5 days.

figures.title: Does a model transfer to another population?
figures.caption: On the other cohort a model is on par with repeating the last value; training or calibrating locally closes the gap.

figures.title: Federated learning (simulated clinics)
figures.caption: Sharing model updates instead of records matches pooled training and beats a clinic alone.

figures.title: Privacy sweep
figures.caption: How accuracy changes as differential-privacy noise is added to federated updates (exploratory).

transfer.title: Local calibration carries a model to a new population
transfer.sub: Cross-cohort transfer on a shared 15-minute grid, mean absolute error at +60 min (mg/dL).
transfer.note: A model trained elsewhere is on par with repeating the last value and 3.4 mg/dL (CI 2.9 to 4.0) behind one trained on the target population. A few days of the new patient's data close part of the gap (calibration with 3 days: −0.83, CI −1.19 to −0.50). The console uses this recipe.

stress.title: Synthetic Indian cohort (simulated)
stress.sub: 100 virtual patients per setting, 10 days, 16 Indian meal presets (carbohydrate from IFCT 2017), insulin sensitivity lowered by 0.46 log units. Models trained on the real cohorts; error at +60 min (mg/dL).
stress.note: With 3 days of calibration the model beats repeating the last value in every setting. Adding synthetic patients to training did not improve results, so the synthetic cohort is used to stress-test and demonstrate, not to train.

federated.title: Federated learning (simulated clinics)
federated.sub: Open-cohort patients grouped into clinics; raw records never leave a clinic, only model updates are shared. Error at +60 min (mg/dL).
federated.note: Federated averaging matches pooled training (difference 0.09 to 0.12, intervals include 0) and beats a small clinic alone by about 2 mg/dL. The privacy design is data minimisation: records stay at the clinic. Formal differential-privacy guarantees need more clinics than a handful, so none is claimed.

sleep.title: Could a model detect an effect of sleep on glucose? (simulated)
sleep.sub: 100 simulated patients, 67,000 scored windows per condition. Sleep shortens each night and lowers insulin sensitivity from 06:00 the next day. m scales the effect (m = 0 is a false-positive control, m = 1 is literature scale). Change in error from adding the sleep channel, mg/dL, 95 % interval.
cols: Mean change in log insulin sensitivity
sleep.note: The control behaves correctly (no false gain), and sleep features add no detectable forecast accuracy even at five times the literature effect; heart rate and activity add nothing either. The console therefore presents sleep, heart rate variability and steps as clinical context.

scale.title: Larger run: 300 simulated patients, 30 days (about 9 times more patient-days)
scale.sub: 777,000 scored windows per condition. Same design; change in error from adding the sleep channel, mg/dL, 95 % interval.
scale.note: The control shows no leak. At literature scale the sleep channel is detectable at +30 minutes, by about 0.06 mg/dL (0.5 % of the forecast error); the console keeps it as context. A simulation result about detectability.
